Wadsworth Center Scientists Publish Genomic Characterization of Drug-Resistant Bacterial Species Causing Urinary Tract Infections

Scientists at the Wadsworth Center's Bacteriology Laboratory recently published findings characterizing the genetic features of a recently identified bacterial species associated with complex urinary tract infections and antimicrobial resistance. Antimicrobial resistance occurs when bacteria acquire the ability to survive exposure to drugs that would normally kill them or inhibit their growth. Resistance to carbapenems, often considered drugs of last resort, is especially concerning because it can severely limit treatment options.

Wadsworth Center Selected to Establish an Interlaboratory Program for Serum PFAS Measurements

The Wadsworth Center’s Division of Environmental Health Sciences (DEHS) has been selected by the Association of Public Health Laboratories to establish an interlaboratory program for serum testing of per- and polyfluoroalkyl substances (PFAS) by U.S. public health laboratories. PFAS, often called “forever chemicals,” can be measured in serum to assess human exposure. Because serum PFAS testing methods are complex and are used primarily for public health surveillance and human biomonitoring, interlaboratory studies are an important way to support consistent, high-quality testing.

Wadsworth Center Newborn Screening Program Contributes to GUARDIAN Genome Sequencing Study

The Wadsworth Center Newborn Screening Program has participated in the GUARDIAN newborn genome sequencing study since 2022. GUARDIAN is a research study that screens newborns for 321 to 465 genetic conditions, most of which are not included in the standard New York State newborn screening process. With informed consent, the GUARDIAN panel is offered to families of newborns delivered at select New York City hospitals. Testing uses DNA extracted from residual blood samples collected for newborn screening, followed by genome sequencing and targeted analysis.

Recent Wadsworth Center Publication Reveals Widespread Drug Occurrence in Wastewater From Rural Central New York

Wastewater-based epidemiology provides a noninvasive, objective way to estimate community-level drug consumption and validate patterns of drug use. Mapping local patterns can help identify high-risk populations, geographic hotspots, and emerging behavioral trends, supporting targeted, evidence-based, and culturally relevant public health interventions. Although widely used in European cities, wastewater surveillance can be especially valuable in rural areas, where access to drug rehabilitation and other services may be limited.
